title: When should I start talking to kids about money?
content:
Most children don't learn about money until it's too late to build real habits. At Grow Good Daily, we believe starting financial education at age 3 changes everything — and the research backs us up.

If you've ever handed your child a dollar at the school fair and watched them spend it on the first shiny thing they saw, you're not alone. Most parents wait until the "right moment" to talk about money — until kids are old enough to understand, responsible enough to care, or old enough to have a job. But here's the truth: by the time that moment feels right, the habits are already forming without you.

Financial habits — the emotional relationship with spending, saving, and patience — begin developing in early childhood. And the earlier you start gentle, age-appropriate conversations about money, the better equipped your child will be for life.

Age 3
When money concepts begin
Age 7
When habits are set
77%
Of adults wish they'd learned earlier
Why Age 3 Is Not Too Young
Research from the University of Cambridge found that money habits and attitudes are largely formed by age 7. That means the window between ages 3 and 7 is a critical, often missed opportunity for parents to lay the groundwork.

At age 3, children already understand the basic concept that things cost something — they've seen you tap a card, pull out a wallet, or say "we can't afford that right now." They're absorbing your relationship with money whether you're teaching them or not. The question isn't whether your children will learn about money from you. It's what they'll learn.

The Grow Good Principle: Children don't need to understand interest rates or investment portfolios. They need to understand that money is a tool — something you earn, choose to spend wisely, and save intentionally. Those values take root early.

A Simple Guide by Age
Financial education doesn't need to be a formal lesson. It's woven into everyday moments — at the grocery store, the piggy bank, the birthday gift budget. Here's what to focus on at each stage:

Ages 3–5
Needs vs. wants
Use simple language at the store. "We need milk, but we want cookies — let's think about it." Introduce a piggy bank with separate sections for spending and saving.

Ages 6–8
Earning and choices
Small chores for small allowances. When they want a toy, let them save for part of it. This teaches delayed gratification in a low-stakes, real way.

Ages 9–12
Budgeting basics
Give them a set amount for school supplies or a category of spending. Let them make choices — and live with them. The lessons from small mistakes are priceless.

Ages 13–17
Real-world money skills
Bank accounts, debit cards, first jobs. Talk about taxes, saving goals, and the difference between good and bad debt. Make it conversational, not a lecture.

The Conversation No One Wants to Have (But Should)
Many parents avoid money talk because they feel their own finances aren't perfect — or because they weren't taught well themselves. We hear this all the time at Grow Good Daily. But here's what we've learned: you don't need to be a financial expert to raise a financially confident child.

You just need to be honest and present.

Narrate your decisions out loud. "I'm choosing the store brand because it's just as good and saves us money for our vacation fund."
Let kids see — and sometimes join — real money decisions appropriate to your family's situation.
Normalize talking about money the same way you talk about health, kindness, or hard work.
Celebrate saving, not just spending. Make the piggy bank a source of pride, not just a slot for coins.
Correct mistakes without shame. A child who spends all their money too fast is learning, not failing.
"The goal isn't to raise a child who never makes financial mistakes. It's to raise a child who has the language, values, and resilience to learn from them."
What Happens When We Wait
When money education is delayed — or never happens — kids fill the gap with what they observe and absorb from culture: social media, peers, advertising. The messages they receive aren't neutral. They're designed by brands to equate spending with happiness, status, and belonging.

Young adults who never learned to save, budget, or distinguish a need from a want don't suddenly develop those skills at 18 or 22. They struggle with credit card debt, impulse spending, and a deep anxiety about finances that often lasts a lifetime.

This isn't a scare tactic — it's a reason to feel empowered. Because you can change this story, starting today, with a simple conversation over breakfast.

Starting Today: Three Things You Can Do This Week
The grocery store game:
Let your child hold the list and compare two prices. Ask: "Which one is the better deal? Why?" No wrong answers — just conversation.
Set up a saving jar:
Even a glass jar with a paper label is powerful. Let your child put coins in and watch it grow. Talk about what they're saving for.
Tell a money story:
Share an age-appropriate story from your own life — a time you saved for something, made a money mistake, or were proud of a financial decision. You're their first and most influential teacher.
You Don't Need to Be Perfect. You Need to Start.
Financial literacy isn't a subject. It's a lifelong practice — and the families who practice it together, openly and without shame, raise children who are genuinely prepared for the world.

At Grow Good Daily, we believe small daily conversations create lasting roots. Money is one of the most powerful tools your child will ever have. Help them understand it, respect it, and use it well — starting now, wherever they are, wherever you are.

Because the best time to start was yesterday. The second best time? This morning, at the breakfast table.
